description: A group that accepts all members in UofT eng who are interested in game programming. We are using Unreal Engine 5 to build games, and previously we have programmed multiple games.
summary:
Our project is an interactive, browser-based Mars outpost game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of living beyond Earth. Players build and manage a small settlement, making decisions about limited resources, growing food, and maintaining power while responding to Martian dust storms.

The game addresses the challenge by turning space exploration concepts into hands-on choices with visible consequences. Rather than simply reading about survival on Mars, players explore how an outpost’s systems depend on one another—for example, how reduced solar power during a dust storm can affect the settlement’s ability to function.

By combining accessible gameplay, an illustrated Martian environment, and scientific learning, our project makes a complex topic approachable for young audiences. It encourages curiosity, systems thinking, and thoughtful decision-making, helping players understand that a sustainable future in space depends on balancing human needs with environmental constraints.
details:
Our project turns the challenge of surviving on Mars into an interactive learning experience for children aged 7–12. In a browser-based game, players manage a small Martian outpost and explore how decisions about power, food production, and limited resources affect the settlement.

How it works:
Players make choices about their outpost and observe the consequences through changes in the game’s resources and environment. Solar panels provide power, while a greenhouse supports food production. Dust storms introduce disruptions that encourage players to reconsider their priorities. These connected systems communicate a central idea: surviving in space requires understanding how individual decisions affect an entire habitat.

The game simplifies these relationships for learning rather than attempting to reproduce a complete engineering simulation. Its purpose is to make the underlying challenges understandable through experimentation.

Benefits and intended impact:
Our intended impact is to help young learners move from curiosity about space to an understanding of the problems future explorers must solve. The experience encourages systems thinking, resource awareness, and decision-making under constraints. Players can learn from setbacks, adjust their approach, and discover why a sustainable settlement needs more than a collection of buildings.

A browser-based format lowers the barrier to participation and makes the project suitable for sharing with families and educators.

Development and tools:
We built the project using HTML-based web development, combining layered static illustrations with lightweight GIF animations. This approach allowed us to create an expressive Martian environment while keeping the prototype manageable within the hackathon timeframe.

Creativity and design considerations:
The project combines the appeal of a survival game with an approachable, illustrated world. Scientific concepts become decisions players can experience: a dust storm becomes a practical challenge to power management, while growing food becomes part of maintaining a functioning outpost.

Our team considered the audience’s age, clarity of instructions, visual feedback, accessibility through a browser, and the balance between educational value and enjoyable gameplay. We aimed to keep choices understandable while preserving meaningful connections between the outpost’s systems. The result is a playful introduction to the planning, interdependence, and care required to sustain human life beyond Earth.
